introduction: “O God, my God! Join in accord these two souls and set firm their feet in eternal love.” These are ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s prayers for couples at their marriage and after it: that the two become “as one body, one soul”, that the bond endure, that their home be blessed with children and their union be a service to God. Genesis says the same in “one flesh” and “bone of my bones”; the Song of Songs and Ruth give the vows; Tobias’s wedding-night prayer and the Qur’an’s “love and mercy between you” are the nearest kin among prayers. Shakespeare’s sonnet wishes the constancy asked for here. Gibran’s “spaces in your togetherness” and Paul’s doubt about the married are the two cautions.
questions: What do these prayers ask God to do, and what do they leave to the couple?
“One body, one soul, and one heart.” What is good in that image, and what does Gibran’s line add?
Several prayers ask that the marriage serve something beyond itself. What might that be for a particular couple?

outside.why: “Join in accord these two souls.” A man shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.
Make these two “even as one body, one soul, and one heart”. They are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.
Make this bond enduring. Let me not to the marriage of true minds admit impediments. Love is not love which alters when it alteration finds.
Gibran’s wish for the married runs the other way: let there be spaces in your togetherness. Is there room for it in a prayer that two become “one soul”?
That this marriage be auspicious and blessed. The prayer of Tobias on his wedding night: mercifully ordain that we may become aged together.
A cause of enduring love. He created for you helpmeets from yourselves that ye might find rest in them, and He ordained between you love and mercy.
Make this marriage the cause of heavenly blessing. At the wedding in Cana the water became wine, and the governor of the feast called the bridegroom to praise it.
“We have become united through love for Thy beauty.” Whither thou goest, I will go; thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God.
Two birds of the celestial gardens. My beloved is mine, and I am his.
From the conjunction of these two stars, may offspring come. Lo, children are an heritage of the Lord.
Two orbs wedded in Thy love and joined in service. Two are better than one; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.
Marriage enjoined, that the generations may succeed one another. It is not good that the man should be alone.
That this marriage may be blessed and happy. Whoso findeth a wife findeth a good thing, and obtaineth favour of the Lord.
Make them as one body and one soul. This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh.
Make firm their feet in Thy love and strengthen their affection. Love is strong as death; many waters cannot quench love.
He has married in obedience to Thy bidding. Marriage is honourable in all.
Thou hast favoured him with one of Thy handmaidens. Rejoice with the wife of thy youth.
Endear this loving handmaid; bless her household. Her children arise up, and call her blessed; her husband also, and he praiseth her.
Thy husband has entered beneath the shade of the Tree. What knowest thou, O wife, whether thou shalt save thy husband?
“Composer of hearts … Gatherer of all pairs.” Our Lord! Vouchsafe us comfort of our wives and of our offspring.
A heavenly blessing on this union. The Lord bless thee, and keep thee; the Lord make his face shine upon thee.
Protect these two birds in the orchard of Thy mercy. Thy wife shall be as a fruitful vine: thy children like olive plants round about thy table.
A servant and a handmaid gathered under one shade. Heirs together of the grace of life; that your prayers be not hindered.
Bind these two souls together. As for me and my house, we will serve the Lord.

Paul doubted that the married can give God their whole care: he that is married careth for the things of the world, how he may please his wife. These prayers ask that the marriage itself be service. Which have you seen?

shortfall: The prayers ask one blessing in closely similar words; four of the twenty-nine were left to share their neighbours’ companions.
